notes:
Task and constraints: Update a Minesweeper board after a click, revealing adjacent mine counts or blank regions.
Idea: Process cells in breadth-first layers, counting adjacent mines and expanding from empty cells with no adjacent mines.
Technique and why it applies: A clicked mine becomes X. Otherwise each queued cell counts neighboring M cells; it becomes a digit when the count is positive, or B and enqueues adjacent E cells when the count is zero. Marking enqueued cells as a space prevents duplicate queue entries.
Invariant: Every cell queued for expansion has already been marked so it cannot be enqueued repeatedly.
Edge cases: The board is assumed nonempty and rectangular. A click on M returns immediately with X. The implementation uses a space as a temporary visited marker, then converts processed cells to B or a digit.
Complexity: Each cell is enqueued and processed at most once, with eight-neighbor checks, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) queue space in the worst case. The author O(m+n) space label understates the possible frontier size.

Task and constraints: Reveal the Minesweeper cell clicked by the player and any blank-connected region.
Idea: Use an explicit stack to reveal cells without recursive calls.
Technique and why it applies: For each popped cell, count neighboring mines and gather neighboring E cells. A positive count writes the digit; zero writes B and marks adjacent empty cells with a space before pushing them, avoiding repeated visits.
Invariant: stk contains cells scheduled for reveal, while processed cells are no longer marked E.
Edge cases: Clicking a mine changes it to X and returns immediately. The implementation assumes a nonempty rectangular board; a space is used as an internal visited marker.
Complexity: Every cell is pushed at most once and each checks eight neighbors, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) worst-case stack space.

Task and constraints: Count unique pairs with absolute difference k in nums.
Idea: Store each encountered value shifted by k and detect when a later value matches that stored key.
Technique and why it applies: When processing n, dict1[n] being present indicates an earlier value n-k was seen. The values are collected in res and converted to a set to avoid counting duplicate pairs multiple times.
Invariant: dict1 maps each value-plus-k to the source value that created that key; res stores candidate larger values with a matching predecessor.
Edge cases: For k=0, repeated occurrences of the same value are detected and counted once after set conversion. Negative k is not handled explicitly and can produce a count even though the standard definition expects k>=0.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), the dictionary pass is O(n) expected, and the final set conversion is O(n) expected. Auxiliary space is O(n).

Task and constraints: Return the number of unique pairs whose values differ by k.
Idea: Use a set of seen values and a set of distinct pair representatives.
Technique and why it applies: When num-k has appeared, the pair is represented by num-k; when num+k has appeared, the pair is represented by num. Sets prevent duplicate values or repeated occurrences from counting the same pair more than once.
Invariant: lookup contains all values processed so far, and result contains distinct representatives of valid pairs.
Edge cases: Negative k returns zero immediately. For k=0, a value is added to result only after the same value has already been seen, counting each duplicated value once.
Complexity: Each input value performs expected O(1) set operations, giving O(n) expected time and O(n) space, matching the labels.

Task and constraints: Multiply two complex numbers supplied as strings in real+imaginaryi format.
Idea: Parse each real and imaginary component, then apply the complex multiplication formula.
Technique and why it applies: For (a+bi)(x+yi), the real part is ax-by and the imaginary part is ay+bx. The code extracts components around '+' and the trailing i, computes both parts, and formats the result.
Invariant: ans1 and ans2 hold the real and imaginary parts of the product respectively.
Edge cases: The string format is assumed to include a plus separator and trailing i. Negative imaginary parts are represented after the plus as a signed integer, so int parsing handles them.
Complexity: Each string is parsed and formatted in O(1) time under bounded integer sizes, with O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the product of two complex numbers encoded as strings.
Idea: Split each string into its real and imaginary integer components and apply the multiplication identity.
Technique and why it applies: The real component is ra*rb - ia*ib, and the imaginary component is ra*ib + ia*rb. The result is formatted back into the required real+imaginaryi form.
Invariant: The parsed pairs represent the two complex operands before the formula is applied.
Edge cases: The strings are assumed to have the specified plus sign and trailing i. Signed integer components are accepted by int().
Complexity: Parsing fixed-format strings and computing two products/sums is O(1) under the problem's bounded inputs; auxiliary space is O(1), matching the labels.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum difference in minutes between any two clock times in 24-hour HH:MM format.
Idea: Convert times to minutes since midnight, sort them, and compare adjacent values plus the wraparound pair.
Technique and why it applies: The sorted order makes the smallest non-circular gap occur between neighbors. The last-to-first gap across midnight is also considered to handle times near 23:59 and 00:00.
Invariant: min_diff is the smallest gap among adjacent sorted times processed so far and the circular boundary gap once evaluated.
Edge cases: Duplicate times yield a zero gap. The code assumes at least one time point; otherwise minutes[-1] and minutes[0] fail.
Complexity: Conversion and sorting take O(n log n), followed by an O(n) scan. The minutes list uses O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the unique element in a sorted array where every other value appears exactly twice.
Idea: Recursively split the array and retain the side whose length parity indicates the singleton.
Technique and why it applies: If the last value of the left half equals the first of the right half, that pair straddles the split and is removed from both halves. The singleton must lie in the remaining odd-length side; the method recurses until one value remains.
Invariant: The chosen recursive subarray contains the unique element and has odd length under the input guarantee.
Edge cases: A one-element list returns directly. The algorithm slices arrays at each level, allocating copies; valid input with exactly one singleton prevents both halves from becoming empty at a boundary pair.
Complexity: The recurrence scans/slices a total O(n) elements across levels in a rough bound, but slicing copies can yield O(n) time and O(n) cumulative allocation; peak auxiliary space can be O(n).

Task and constraints: Reverse the first k characters of every 2k block in s, leaving the following k characters unchanged.
Idea: Convert s to a mutable character list and reverse each k-sized slice at starts spaced 2k apart.
Technique and why it applies: The slice assignment replaces the first half of each block with its reversed copy. Slices shorter than k at the end are reversed as they are.
Invariant: After each iteration, the first k characters of that 2k segment are reversed and earlier segments remain finalized.
Edge cases: If the final segment has fewer than k characters, all of them are reversed. The code prints the character list, producing unwanted debug output.
Complexity: Each character participates in a constant amount of slicing and assignment, so time is O(n) and auxiliary storage is O(n) for the list and slices.

Task and constraints: Reverse the first k characters in every block of 2k characters.
Idea: Convert to a list and reverse each selected slice in place.
Technique and why it applies: The loop visits starts 0, 2k, 4k, and so on; reversed(s[i:i+k]) produces the reversed prefix of each block while leaving the second half untouched.
Invariant: Every processed 2k block has its first k characters reversed and all later blocks remain unchanged.
Edge cases: A short final slice is reversed completely. k must be positive because the range step is 2*k.
Complexity: The characters are processed in O(n) time. The list conversion and returned string require O(n) space, so the author O(1) space label omits the working copy and output.

Task and constraints: For each matrix cell, return the distance to the nearest zero using four-directional moves.
Idea: Initialize all zero cells as multi-source BFS starting points and assign a large provisional distance to ones.
Technique and why it applies: BFS expands outward from every zero. A neighbor is updated only when its current distance exceeds the popped cell's distance plus one, so the first shortest path establishes the nearest-zero distance.
Invariant: queue holds cells whose distance can improve neighboring cells, and matrix stores the best distance found so far.
Edge cases: Empty matrix or empty first row returns an empty list. The code references deque without importing it, so it fails unless deque is defined externally. It mutates the input matrix.
Complexity: Each cell can be improved/enqueued under BFS distance ordering, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) queue space in the worst case.

Task and constraints: Compute each cell's shortest Manhattan distance to a zero in a binary matrix.
Idea: Use two DP sweeps, first top-left to bottom-right and then bottom-right to top-left.
Technique and why it applies: The forward pass propagates distances from top and left neighbors; the reverse pass propagates from bottom and right neighbors. Taking the minimum across these directions captures shortest paths to zeros.
Invariant: After the first pass, dp contains best paths using top/left directions; after the second, it includes the other two directions.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty matrix because it accesses matrix[0]. It returns a separate dp matrix rather than modifying the input.
Complexity: Two complete matrix scans take O(mn) time and the DP table uses O(mn) space, matching the labels.

Task and constraints: Return the distance to the nearest zero for each cell in a binary matrix.
Idea: Seed a queue with all zeros and propagate distance values outward through neighboring cells.
Technique and why it applies: Ones are initialized to infinity. A neighbor is enqueued only when the current cell's distance plus one improves its value, which propagates shortest distances from the multi-source zero frontier.
Invariant: Each matrix value is the best distance found so far; queue entries identify cells that may improve adjacent values.
Edge cases: The code assumes matrix has at least one row and column. It mutates matrix in place and returns it.
Complexity: Under FIFO BFS from all zero sources, each cell receives its shortest distance and is processed with four neighbor checks, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) worst-case queue space.

Task and constraints: Find the nearest-zero distance for every cell using two directional passes.
Idea: Initialize each one from its top and left neighbors, then refine it using bottom and right neighbors in reverse order.
Technique and why it applies: Distances can be propagated along shortest Manhattan paths in either direction. The forward pass establishes paths from above/left zeros, and the reverse pass incorporates paths from below/right zeros.
Invariant: Each update lowers a nonzero cell's distance to the best path discovered through the processed directions.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty rectangular matrix. It overwrites the input cells with distances, preserving zeros.
Complexity: Two scans visit every cell once, so time is O(mn). The matrix itself serves as the DP table, giving O(1) additional space beyond the input.

Task and constraints: Maximize points earned by removing contiguous groups of same-colored boxes, scoring the square of the group size.
Idea: Use memoized interval DP with an extra parameter k for boxes of the left color already attached from outside the interval.
Technique and why it applies: The default choice removes the current run immediately for (k+1)^2 points. Alternative choices delay removing that color and merge it with a matching box at index m after clearing the intervening interval.
Invariant: dp(i,j,k) is the best score for boxes i through j when k matching boxes are attached to the left.
Edge cases: An empty interval returns zero. The snippet uses lru_cache without importing it, so it fails unless that decorator is defined externally.
Complexity: There are O(n³) states and each may scan O(n) matching positions, giving O(n⁴) worst-case time and O(n³) memo space.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum score from repeatedly removing contiguous groups of equal-colored boxes.
Idea: Memoize a three-parameter DFS over interval endpoints and the count of same-colored boxes carried into the interval.
Technique and why it applies: The loop first merges adjacent boxes equal to boxes[l] into k. It then compares removing that run now against clearing an intervening interval and merging with a later matching box.
Invariant: lookup[l][r][k] stores the best score for interval [l,r] with k same-colored boxes joined to its left.
Edge cases: An empty interval returns zero. The memo is initialized with zeros, which is safe because nonempty intervals have positive optimal scores under the standard positive scoring rule.
Complexity: The DP uses O(n³) space. Each state may scan O(n) matching positions, so O(n⁴) worst-case time is a safe bound; the author's range O(n³)~O(n⁴) reflects this.

Task and constraints: Count connected components, called provinces, in an undirected city adjacency matrix.
Idea: Build adjacency lists and run DFS from each city not yet visited.
Technique and why it applies: Starting a DFS explores every city connected to the chosen city, marking neighbors visited. Each new unvisited city starts another component and increments the count.
Invariant: visit contains cities already reached from prior component searches.
Edge cases: The code references defaultdict without importing it, so it fails unless that name is available externally. Isolated cities are not inserted as graph keys but are still counted when the outer loop reaches them.
Complexity: Building the graph scans the n×n matrix, and DFS visits each city and edge, giving O(n²) time and O(n²) adjacency storage.

Task and constraints: Check whether an attendance record contains fewer than two absences and no three consecutive late marks.
Idea: Scan all length-three slices for LLL and count occurrences of A.
Technique and why it applies: Any triple equal to LLL violates the late rule, and two or more A characters violate the absence rule. eligible remains False once either violation is found.
Invariant: eligible represents whether no violation has been discovered, while absent counts absence markers.
Edge cases: Strings shorter than three skip the triple scan. The code continues counting after a violation but returns the same False result.
Complexity: Slice comparisons and the absence count each scan O(n) characters, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return whether the attendance string has at most one A and no LLL substring.
Idea: Count absences while scanning, and test each position for a triple of consecutive L characters.
Technique and why it applies: The method returns False immediately on the second A or on a detected LLL run. If the full scan completes, neither rule was violated.
Invariant: count_A is the number of absences seen so far; every triple beginning at or before i has been checked as the scan advances.
Edge cases: Empty strings return True. The i < len(s)-2 guard prevents indexing beyond the end when checking three consecutive characters.
Complexity: One scan with constant-time checks gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, matching the labels.

Task and constraints: Count valid attendance records of length n modulo 10^9+7, allowing at most one absence and at most two consecutive lates.
Idea: Model six attendance states as a fixed transition matrix and raise it to the nth power by repeated squaring.
Technique and why it applies: The matrix encodes transitions between states for absence count and trailing late count. power computes the matrix exponent using binary exponentiation, and multiplying by initial_counts yields state counts for length n.
Invariant: Each exponentiation step accumulates powers of the transition matrix corresponding to processed exponent bits.
Edge cases: The code depends on NumPy being installed. The initial vector and transition matrix encode the state ordering, so correctness depends on that correspondence. n=0 returns the initial-state count sum.
Complexity: Matrix exponentiation takes O(log n) multiplications of fixed 6×6 matrices, effectively O(log n) time and O(1) space under the fixed state dimension, though NumPy objects are allocated.
